title: Noise-cancelling headphones
caption: Your headphones fight noise with *more* noise. 🎧
The trick is a mirror-image sound wave.
send: Send this to the friend who wears headphones 24/7.

beats.say: Your headphones kill noise — by making more noise.
Tiny mics on the outside... listen to the world.
Sound is a wave — pushing and pulling the air.
So a chip builds the exact opposite wave.
But here's the twist... the speaker plays it back.
Push meets pull — and they cancel out. Silence.

title: How planes stay up
caption: Engines don't lift a jet. Something else does. ✈️
It's all about where the air goes.
send: Send this to the friend who's scared of flying.

beats.say: Jet engines don't hold planes up.
The wings do — tilted just a few degrees.
So they shove tons of air downward... every second.
Push air down — and the air pushes the wing up.
But that's only half of it... pressure above the wing drops.
Spread over 800 square metres, that lifts hundreds of tons.
The engines? They just keep it fast enough.

title: The QR code's origin
caption: The QR code wasn't made for menus. It was made for car parts. 🚗
And its idea came from an ancient board game.
send: Send this to the friend who scans every QR code.

beats.say: A Japanese car-parts factory invented the code you scan daily.
Back in 1994, its workers were drowning in barcodes.
But a barcode only holds about 20 characters.
So engineer Masahiro Hara found an idea — in the board game Go.
Black and white squares... readable from any angle.
It can lose 30% of itself — and still work.
So next time you scan a menu, remember —

title: How a fridge makes cold
caption: Your fridge has never made cold. Not once. 🧊
It's a heat thief, and the back of it proves it.
send: Send this to the friend who stands with the fridge door open.

beats.say: Your fridge doesn't make cold... it steals heat.
A liquid in its pipes boils — even below freezing.
Boiling soaks up heat, so your food gets cold.
But that heat has to go somewhere.
So a pump squeezes the gas until it's hot.
Then the coils on the back... dump it into your kitchen.

title: How Face ID sees you
caption: Every unlock fires 30,000 invisible dots at your face. 📱
That's why a photo of you can't open your phone.
send: Send this to the friend who unlocks their phone 100 times a day.

beats.say: Your phone sprays your face with 30,000 invisible dots.
They're infrared — so your eyes can't see them.
But a tiny camera can.
On a curved face... the dots stretch and bunch up.
That pattern becomes a 3D map of you.
So a flat photo can't fool it — it has no depth.
Every unlock, without you noticing —

title: How solar panels work
caption: A solar panel has zero moving parts. ☀️
So how does sunlight become power?
send: Send this to the friend who wants solar panels.

beats.say: Solar panels make power — with zero moving parts.
Each one is a slice of silicon... in two layers.
Sunlight hits it — and knocks electrons loose.
But loose electrons just wander around.
So the layers push them one way... and that's a current.
Most panels turn about a fifth of sunlight into power.
That's how, every sunny day,

title: How websites check passwords
caption: A well-built website never knows your password. 🔑
Here's how it still knows when you type it right.
send: Send this to the friend who uses the same password everywhere.

beats.say: Good websites don't know your password.
They scramble it with a hash — a one-way blender.
Same password, same scramble... every single time.
But you can't unscramble it. Not even the website can.
So when you log in, it scrambles your guess — and compares.
Hackers steal scrambles, not passwords... unless yours is short.

title: What lightning really is
caption: A lightning bolt is hotter than the surface of the Sun. ⚡
And it all starts with ice.
send: Send this to the friend who loves thunderstorms.

beats.say: A lightning bolt is five times hotter than the Sun's surface.
It starts inside a storm cloud... with ice.
Ice crystals smash together and swap electric charge.
But the charges split up — plus on top, minus below.
So the air finally breaks... and a giant spark jumps.
It heats the air so fast, it explodes. That's thunder.

title: How streaming works
caption: Streaming apps never send you the whole movie. 🎬
That's the secret to never buffering.
send: Send this to the friend who blames the Wi-Fi for everything.

beats.say: Streaming apps never send you the whole movie.
They chop it into chunks — just a few seconds each.
Each chunk is saved in many qualities.
But your internet speed keeps changing.
So your player checks it... before every single chunk.
Slow? The next chunk gets blurrier — instead of freezing.
That's why, even on bad Wi-Fi,

title: How rainbows work
caption: You'll never see a rainbow facing the Sun. 🌈
And every rainbow is secretly a full circle.
send: Send this to the friend who stops the car for rainbows.

beats.say: You can only see a rainbow with the Sun behind you.
Every raindrop acts like a tiny prism.
Sunlight bends in — and bounces off the back.
But each color bends a different amount.
So the light comes back at exactly 42 degrees.
That's why it's a circle... the ground just hides half.
So next time it rains — remember,

title: What charging really does
caption: Charging your phone doesn't pour electricity into it. 🔋
It moves atoms, and every trip wears them out.
send: Send this to the friend who charges to 100% every night.

beats.say: Charging your phone doesn't fill it with electricity.
It moves lithium ions from one side to the other.
They squeeze between layers of graphite... and wait.
Unplug, and they rush back — powering your phone.
But every trip wears the battery down.
Heat and 100% make it worse... so stop at 80.

title: How wireless charging works
caption: Your wireless charger never touches your battery. ⚡
It throws power through thin air, using magnets.
send: Send this to the friend whose phone never charges on the pad.

beats.say: Your wireless charger never touches your battery.
There's a copper coil in the pad... and one in your phone.
Power flips back and forth through the pad's coil.
So it makes a magnetic field that keeps changing.
That field pushes current into your phone's coil.
But move it a few millimetres — and it fails.

title: Why it's called Bluetooth
caption: Bluetooth is named after a 10th-century Viking king. 👑
And it was only ever meant to be a placeholder.
send: Send this to the friend whose earbuds never connect.

beats.say: Your earbuds' connection is named after a Viking king.
King Harald "Bluetooth" united Danish tribes in the 900s.
In 1997, engineers needed a code name — fast.
Their tech would unite phones and computers... like Harald united tribes.
But the code name was only meant to be temporary.
It stuck. Even the logo is his initials — in runes.
Which is why, a thousand years later,

title: How search is so fast
caption: When you hit search, nothing searches the internet. 🔍
It was all done before you even typed.
send: Send this to the friend who googles everything.

beats.say: When you hit search, nothing searches the internet.
Bots already crawled billions of pages — days ago.
They built an index, like the back of a book.
But that index is too huge for one computer.
So thousands of machines each check their own slice.
Then hundreds of signals rank results — in half a second.
So, believe it or not —

title: How your browser finds a site
caption: Your browser can't read website names. 🌐
Every link you tap starts with a lookup in the internet's phone book.
send: Send this to the friend who thinks the internet is magic.

beats.say: Your browser can't read website names.
Computers only find each other by numbers.
So it asks the internet's phone book — DNS.
But no single server knows every address.
So it asks step by step — root, dot com, then the site.
The number comes back in milliseconds... and gets remembered.
Every time you type one in,

title: How your phone knows which way is up
caption: There's a weight smaller than a grain of sand inside your phone. 📱
It's how your screen knows when to rotate.
send: Send this to the friend whose screen rotates at the worst time.

beats.say: There's a tiny weight bouncing around inside your phone.
It's smaller than a grain of sand.
It hangs on microscopic springs, carved into silicon.
Tilt your phone — and the weight shifts a little.
But it can't feel spinning. So a gyroscope helps.
Together they rotate your screen and count your steps.

title: The internet under the sea
caption: Your messages don't fly through space. They swim. 🌊
Almost all data between continents runs along the ocean floor.
send: Send this to the friend who thinks the internet comes from satellites.

beats.say: Your messages don't travel through space.
Almost all data between continents goes under the sea.
Through cables as thin as a garden hose.
But they carry it as pulses of light.
Over a million kilometres of them — circling the planet.
Satellites? They carry only a tiny share.

title: How barcodes work
caption: A barcode has no idea what the price is. 🏷️
That's how stores change prices without reprinting a thing.
send: Send this to the friend who always uses self-checkout.

beats.say: A barcode doesn't know the price.
It's just a number, written in black and white bars.
The scanner's light bounces off the white gaps.
But misreads happen — so the last digit is a check.
Then the store's computer looks that number up.
That's how prices change — without new barcodes.
So at the checkout, remember —

title: How night mode works
caption: Night mode doesn't take one photo. It takes dozens. 🌙
Then it blends them into one clean shot.
send: Send this to the friend who takes 50 photos of the moon.

beats.say: Night mode doesn't take one photo. It takes dozens.
In the dark, tiny sensors catch barely any light.
So one shot looks grainy and noisy.
Instead, the phone fires a burst while you hold still.
It lines up every frame, pixel by pixel.
Noise cancels out — but real detail adds up.
Every time you shoot after dark,

title: How maps know about traffic
caption: Your map knows about traffic jams because of strangers' phones. 🚗
Every slow car is quietly reporting.
send: Send this to the friend who's always stuck in traffic.

beats.say: Your map knows about traffic because of other people's phones.
Phones in moving cars quietly share their speed.
It's anonymous — just dots moving along roads.
But when hundreds of dots slow to walking pace...
That road turns red.
It mixes in old traffic patterns — and finds you a shortcut.
So when the road turns red —

title: Why there are two tides a day
caption: The Moon pulls the ocean, so why are there two high tides a day? 🌙
Because it also pulls the Earth away from the water.
send: Send this to the friend who loves the beach.

beats.say: There are two high tides a day, not one.
The Moon's gravity pulls the ocean toward it.
But it pulls the near side harder than the far side.
So Earth gets stretched — into two ocean bulges.
As Earth spins, your coast passes through both.
That takes about 24 hours and 50 minutes.

title: How Wi-Fi works
caption: Wi-Fi is just radio, like the one in your car. 📶
So how does it carry a whole movie?
send: Send this to the friend who restarts the router for everything.

beats.say: Wi-Fi is just radio — the same as your car radio.
But it shouts much faster — billions of waves a second.
Your router turns data into tiny wave changes.
Each pattern carries ten bits at once.
So your phone catches the waves — and decodes them.
Multiple antennas send at once, like extra highway lanes.
